raw_case_text:
A 56-year-old male visited his primary care physician to be evaluated for abdominal pain, and the subsequent workup revealed a large retroperitoneal mass measuring 21.8 x 17.5 x 11 cm. A diagnostic workup revealed a poorly differentiated germ cell neoplasm, most likely an embryonal carcinoma. Two months after his initial presentation he began chemotherapy (bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin). By day 10 of cycle 3 (approximately 4 months after initial presentation), imaging showed a drastic decrease in tumor size.
Six days after his most recent dose of chemotherapy, he presented to the emergency department noting intermittent fatigue, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea since his last chemotherapy treatment. He also noted headache and fever over the past day. In the emergency department (hospital day 0), he was found to be neutropenic with a total white blood cell (WBC) count of 0.6 x 109 cells/l and an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 0.4 x 109 cells/l. He appeared to be in no acute distress but febrile with a temperature of 38.7 C. No obvious signs of an infectious source were noted, including examination of his port-a-cath. The patient was started on cefepime and admitted to the inpatient oncology service for treatment of neutropenic fever.
The admitting physician noted tachycardia, but the patient's blood pressure was within normal limits. The only possible localizing sign of infection was a questionable cellulitis of the right lower leg. As the patient had previously been on prophylactic levofloxacin and had frequently been to infusion clinics, vancomycin was added for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus coverage. The patient was also started on G-CSF (480 mug/day) for neutropenia. Over the subsequent 2 days, his fever and tachycardia continued, and on hospital day 3 the patient became lethargic and confused. A chest radiograph (which showed no sign of pneumonia), blood and urine cultures and a CT scan of the head without contrast showed no acute changes. Throughout this period his ANC remained <1.0 x 109 cells/l.
By hospital day 4, the patient was unable to respond to commands and was transferred to our institution for further care; his WBC count had risen to 1.8 x 109 cells/l (ANC not measured) and he remained febrile. His vancomycin was continued while cefepime was changed to ceftazidime out of concern for cefepime-induced encephalopathy; G-CSF was continued. Shortly after arrival, the patient had 2 tonic clonic seizures, and lorazepam and fosphenytoin were given. He became more lethargic, with periods of apnea, and was transferred to the intensive care unit for endotracheal intubation. An MRI of the brain and MRA of the brain and neck with and without contrast showed an acute punctate infarct in the right hippocampus and no major vascular findings. Continuous EEG monitoring was started. His WBC count shortly after intubation was 11.4 x 109 cells/l with an ANC of 7.0 x 109 cells/l. Fig. 1 shows ANC, WBC count, G-CSF dosing and the patient's symptoms over time.
A lumbar puncture was performed on hospital day 5 and revealed 64 WBC/mul, 30% neutrophils, 39% lymphocytes, glucose 37 mg/dl and protein 99 mg/dl. No organisms were seen on Gram staining. No cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure was measured. A thorough cerebrospinal fluid workup for infection was sent for evaluation, and empiric acyclovir was started. Cerebrospinal fluid India ink stain was completed in the early evening of hospital day 5 and showed rare encapsulated yeast, and the cerebrospinal fluid cryptococcal antigen (Latex Agglutination, IMMY, Inc., Norman, Okla., USA) was positive at a dilution of 1:32.
The infectious disease service was informed of the result, amphotericin B lipid complex was started at a dose of 5 mg/kg, and flucytosine 100 mg/kg/day was also ordered but was not but available until hospital day 7. On hospital day 6, the WBC count rose to 28.0 x 109 cells/l and G-CSF, acyclovir, ceftazidime and vancomycin were stopped.
Throughout hospital days 6 and 7, the patient was minimally responsive despite no sedation since intubation; however, he did withdraw from painful stimuli. No additional seizures occurred. On hospital day 8, the patient moved his lower extremities on command, and his neurological function rapidly improved. Repeat lumbar puncture was performed on hospital day 9 with an opening pressure of 16 cm H20. By hospital day 10, the patient's neurologic status had improved, and he was extubated. His culture showed Cryptococcus neoformans resistant to flucytosine, and so flucytosine was replaced with fluconazole 800 mg daily.
After 14 days total of amphotericin-based combination therapy, the patient continued on fluconazole 800 mg daily consolidation monotherapy. Repeat lumbar puncture at the time of stopping amphotericin showed a decreased cryptococcal antigen titer of 1:4 and an opening pressure of 22 cm H20. On hospital day 21, the patient was discharged to a transitional care unit. Since hospital discharge, the patient has continued to do well in terms of his CM, although he has required hospitalization for pericarditis. He is being maintained on fluconazole 200 mg daily for secondary prophylaxis, and further chemotherapy has been postponed pending improvement of his other health issues.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old male undergoing chemotherapy for retroperitoneal embryonal carcinoma presented with a 1-day history of fever and headache and a 6-day history of fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Four months prior to admission, the patient was diagnosed with a large (21.8 x 17.5 x 11 cm) retroperitoneal poorly differentiated germ cell tumor (embryonal carcinoma) and started on bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin chemotherapy. Six days after completing cycle 3 of chemotherapy, he presented to the emergency department with post-chemotherapy fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, accompanied by 1 day of fever and headache.
subjective.past_medical_history: Retroperitoneal poorly differentiated germ cell neoplasm (embryonal carcinoma) on cycle 3 of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin chemotherapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, headache, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Recent medications: bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin, and prophylactic levofloxacin.

objective.physical_examination: Admission temperature 38.7 C, tachycardia, normal blood pressure, clean port-a-cath site, and questionable right lower leg cellulitis. Progressed to lethargy and confusion on hospital day 3, and unresponsiveness, two generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and apnea requiring endotracheal intubation on hospital day 4.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission neutropenia with WBC 0.6 x 10^9/L and ANC 0.4 x 10^9/L (rising under G-CSF therapy to WBC 1.8 x 10^9/L on day 4, WBC 11.4 x 10^9/L and ANC 7.0 x 10^9/L post-intubation, and WBC 28.0 x 10^9/L on day 6). Chest X-ray and blood and urine cultures were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Day 3 non-contrast head CT was normal; day 4 brain/neck MRI and MRA showed a punctate acute right hippocampal infarct without major vascular abnormality. Day 5 lumbar puncture (coinciding with G-CSF-induced neutrophil recovery) revealed WBC 64/uL (30% neutrophils, 39% lymphocytes), protein 99 mg/dL, glucose 37 mg/dL, negative Gram stain, positive CSF India ink stain showing rare encapsulated yeast, positive CSF cryptococcal antigen (1:32 by latex agglutination), and CSF culture growing flucytosine-resistant Cryptococcus neoformans (subsequent opening pressures 16 cmH2O on day 9 and 22 cmH2O at end of induction with CrAg titer 1:4).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis unmasked by G-CSF-induced neutrophil reconstitution following chemotherapy-induced febrile neutropenia, confirmed by CSF India ink staining, CSF CrAg latex agglutination titer of 1:32, and CSF fungal culture isolating flucytosine-resistant C. neoformans. Initially treated empirically with cefepime (switched to ceftazidime), vancomycin, acyclovir, G-CSF (480 ug/day), lorazepam, and fosphenytoin; upon CM diagnosis on day 5, G-CSF and empiric antibacterials/antivirals were stopped and amphotericin B lipid complex (5 mg/kg/day) plus flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day, switched to oral fluconazole 800 mg/day on day 10 due to flucytosine resistance) were administered for 14 days, resulting in rapid neurological recovery and extubation on day 10, followed by discharge on day 21 on fluconazole consolidation (800 mg/day) and secondary prophylaxis (200 mg/day).
